fact: Larimer County's 2026 fee schedule, which covers both its landfills and its transfer station, prices dirt and sod as rubble at $40 a cubic yard plus the state surcharge, measuring cubic yards as length times width times height in feet divided by 27.
quote: Rubble (concrete, dirt, sod, asphalt, tree trunks, sludge, non-friable asbestos, and other materials) >1,000 lbs per cubic yard … $40 per cubic yard + CO surcharge … To calculate cubic yards = (L x W x H) in feet / 27 … The pricing listed is for both Landfills and the Transfer Station.
source_label: Larimer County Solid Waste, 2026 Landfill Fee Schedule
notes: curl gets a 403 (Cloudflare); read 2026-09-25 through WebFetch twice, the second time asking for the rows character for character. The schedule does not say which county site takes rubble; the county landfill closed August 3, 2026 and disposal moved to the Central Diversion & Transfer Station (larimer.gov/solidwaste). Fees change yearly: re-read in a browser by the recheck date.

fact: Motz, an infill maker, says a professional-level backyard putting green generally costs 20 to 50% more than one made for leisure, largely because of the type and amount of materials, and that apart from the level of detail the biggest cost difference is often the type of turf.
quote: The pricing fluctuation largely comes down to the type and amount of materials used — in the next section, we’ll answer the age-old question: which is better, nylon or poly putting greens? — but in general, a professional-level backyard putting green will cost you anywhere from 20 to 50% more than one made for leisure. … Outside of your desired detail level, the biggest cost difference often comes down to the type of artificial turf you use.
source_label: Motz infill blog, artificial grass for a putting green (April 15, 2020, updated May 15, 2024)
notes: Section "#4 Cost of an artificial putting green", read with curl 2026-09-25. The same paragraph repeats third-party dollar figures; this guide uses only the percentage. Label avoids the post title's superlative, which the copy checker bans.

fact: Motz lists multiple holes, water hazards, bunkers, sand traps, lighting fixtures and green contours among the details that add to a backyard putting green's cost.
quote: Details can add to your cost as well, and there’s no shortage of them to choose from. Depending on your budget, you could add a layer of challenge or visual landscaping interest to your artificial putting green with everything from multiple holes and water hazards to bunkers, sand traps, lighting fixtures, and green contours.
source_label: Motz infill blog, artificial grass for a putting green (April 15, 2020, updated May 15, 2024)

fact: Motz says nylon putting turf resists abrasion better than polypropylene, is often favored by golf pros, and costs more.
quote: Nylon is commonly found in larger-scale artificial turf applications where high foot traffic is expected. With more resilient fibers that offer greater abrasion resistance than poly fibers, nylon is often favored by golf pros and is, relatedly, more expensive.
source_label: Motz infill blog, artificial grass for a putting green (April 15, 2020, updated May 15, 2024)

fact: Motz recommends a texturized putting turf with a short pile of 3/8 to 5/8 inch, about 1/2 inch, for a backyard putting green.
quote: the best type of artificial grass for a backyard putting green is texturized ; has a short pile (or height of turf blade), with a height of 3/8” to 5/8” (or 1/2”)
source_label: Motz infill blog, artificial grass for a putting green (April 15, 2020, updated May 15, 2024)
notes: The quote's superlative is Motz's; the guide copy paraphrases the pile range only.

fact: Motz says a professional-style putting green needs 5 to 7 pounds of infill per square foot, while a recreational green takes 2 to 4 pounds.
quote: Professional-style putting greens require a ballast, five to seven pounds of turf infill per square foot. … If you’re building a recreational putting green, you can plan to use two to four pounds of Envirofill per square foot.
source_label: Motz infill blog, artificial grass for a putting green (April 15, 2020, updated May 15, 2024)
notes: The professional-style rate is followed in the source by a separate top dressing of about one pound per square foot; the worked example uses the 5 to 7 pounds only.

fact: Motz says a recreational putting green's crimped fibers make it easier to keep, with no routine rolling, while a professional-level green needs more grooming, brushing and leveling of its infill over time.
quote: Recreational: Synthetic turf putting greens used for leisure are easier to maintain than professional-level greens because the turf fibers are crimped (textured). There’s no routine maintenance to roll the turf, since you can’t adjust the turf fiber on this type of system. … Competitive players are usually more meticulous and their greens endure more usage, meaning a professional-level green is going to require more surface grooming, brushing, and leveling out of the infill layers over time.
source_label: Motz infill blog, artificial grass for a putting green (April 15, 2020, updated May 15, 2024)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist recommends a compacted base of 3/4-inch rock at least 6 inches thick under a backyard green, because runoff from around the green seeps under it and causes settling, then 3/8-inch minus on top to shape the undulations to the golfer's design.
quote: A PGA-level green starts with proper excavation and base prep. To prevent future surface movement, you will need a solid, compacted aggregate base. I recommend installing a ¾” aggregate rock base with a minimum thickness of 6 inches. Exterior runoff and areas outside the putting green often seep in and below the surface, leading to settling and depressions. … After the drainage rock is installed and compacted, I recommend using a high-quality 3/8” minus material to create your undulations and smooth contouring. … The key is to smoothly shape the underside to match the design and the golfer’s needs.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How to Make Your Backyard Putting Green PGA-Level Quality (JW's installer column, April 30, 2026)
notes: Read with curl 2026-09-25. One distributor's recommendation, not a standard.

fact: The same columnist recommends setting putting green cups in concrete, performance concrete where frost heave is high, because cups set in compacted dirt shift as rain, foot traffic and pulling the flag loosen the soil.
quote: I highly recommend placing putting green cups in concrete. And for areas that have high frost-heave, please use performance concrete. When placing putting green cups in compacted dirt, the cups tend to shift due to loosening soil caused by rainwater, foot traffic, and excessively pulling the flag in and out of the cup.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How to Make Your Backyard Putting Green PGA-Level Quality (JW's installer column, April 30, 2026)

fact: The columnist recommends an all-infill green such as SGW's True Putt for a surface that holds a shot from 100 yards, and says its installation is more complex.
quote: And for a PGA-level experience with a surface that accurately holds a shot from 100 yards away, I recommend SGW’s True Putt, an all-infill professional golf green material. While True Putt installation is more complex, it replicates a natural golf green suitable for chipping and long shots.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How to Make Your Backyard Putting Green PGA-Level Quality (JW's installer column, April 30, 2026)

fact: Southwest Greens, a putting green builder, says a green's cost depends on its design complexity and on site access, that obstacles needing manual labor and unexpected grading raise it, and that its size-based pricing leaves out site preparation, which may include disposing of existing grass or soil.
quote: The cost of your dream backyard putting green depends on its design complexity and required craftsmanship. … The ease of access of your location to our equipment and materials significantly impacts the cost of installation. If large equipment has to avoid obstacles that need more manual labor, expenses may be higher. Further, the need for unexpected grading and site preparation can impact the overall cost. … The cost of site preparation is not included in our size-based pricing. Disposal of existing grass or soil may be required, depending on your location.
source_label: Southwest Greens, Cost of a Backyard Putting Green
notes: Read with curl 2026-09-25; the page is undated.

fact: Southwest Greens' published size bands price greens under 400 square feet higher per square foot than greens of 400 to 2,000 square feet, and those higher than greens of 2,000 square feet and more.
quote: Our pricing structure adapts to virtually any size and is contingent to access. … 2,000 square feet and above: $20 to $25 per sq. ft. 400 - 2,000 square feet: $25 to $30 per sq. ft. Under 400 square feet: $30 to $35 per sq. ft.
source_label: Southwest Greens, Cost of a Backyard Putting Green
notes: The dollar bands stay in the record so the fact can be checked; the guide prints only the direction (smaller greens cost more per square foot) and no dollar figure, per the brief (no prices until Brian approves them; no non-regional price surveys). Tour Greens' page shows the same pattern.

fact: Tour Greens, a putting green maker, says costs can be higher when machines cannot reach the site and the crew has to use wheelbarrows and small equipment, and that significant grading, sodding, retaining walls or other landscaping to prepare and finish the land have a major impact on the price.
quote: The accessibility of the site to equipment and materials can have a major impact on the time and costs involved to install a green. Costs can be higher if the space cannot be accessed with larger machines as we have to use wheelbarrows and small equipment. Similarly, the need for significant grading and sodding or the addition of retaining walls or other landscaping to prepare and finish the land will have a major impact on the price.
source_label: Tour Greens, What Does a Backyard Putting Green Cost (7 Key Factors)
notes: Read with curl 2026-09-25. The page title carries the year 2025 and the page quotes per-square-foot prices; neither is used.

fact: Tour Greens says many owners add multiple cuts of fringe and fairway turf to practice every kind of shot, and that features such as bunkers, tee boxes, dry creeks and water hazards may not change the cost of the green but do change the cost of the whole project.
quote: many people will opt to outfit their green with multiple cuts of fringe and fairway turf so that they can practice all types of shots. … it only takes a few minutes looking through our portfolio of work before they start inquiring about bunkers, tee boxes, dry creeks, water hazards and other cool features. These may not affect the cost of the green, but they do have an impact on the cost of the entire project.
source_label: Tour Greens, What Does a Backyard Putting Green Cost (7 Key Factors)

fact: Tour Greens sells DIY putting green kits built on interlocking base panels, from about 200 to 500 square feet.
quote: We also offer DIY putting green kits featuring interlocking base panels. These putting greens range in size from about 200 to 500 square feet …
source_label: Tour Greens, What Does a Backyard Putting Green Cost (7 Key Factors)
notes: The sentence goes on to give a per-square-foot kit price, cut here and not used.

fact: SYNLawn Golf's GreenMaker putting green kits assemble on foam base panels on any flat surface.
quote: … Putting Green Kit with our exclusive Precision Putt® putting surface for true ball roll assembles in minutes on any flat surface. … The proprietary Berrasof Core foam base panels provide a stable foundation and realistic feel.
source_label: SYNLawn Golf, Products (GreenMaker putting green kits)
notes: Read with curl and a browser user agent 2026-09-25 (a bare user agent gets a 403). Kit prices on the page are not used.

fact: SYNLawn's do-it-yourself guide for lawn turf has the owner dig out 3 to 4 inches for the base, estimates about 1 ton of base per 100 square feet at 3 inches and 13 to 16 wheelbarrow loads per ton, and recommends 1 to 2 pounds of sand infill per square foot.
quote: Note: You will need about 1 ton of aggregate or base material for every 100 sq. ft. at a 3” depth. … For each ton of aggregate, you are looking at approximately 13-16 wheelbarrows full that will need to be hauled to the project area from the staged dumping area. … Depending on your area, you will need to remove between 3”- 4” to create an adequate drainage base. … We recommend about 1-2 lbs. of sand per sq. ft., depending on the application and the product.
source_label: SYNLawn DIY Installation Guidelines (2013 revision), Lowe's product document
notes: PDF read with pdftotext 2026-09-25 (document title rev.4.8.13, created April 2013). Written for lawn turf, not putting greens.

fact: Arithmetic on published rules of thumb, not a measured job: for 500 square feet, a 3-inch lawn base takes about 5 tons of rock (65 to 80 wheelbarrow loads) and digs out about 4.6 cubic yards, about $185 at Larimer County's $40 rubble rate, while a 6-inch green base takes about 10 tons (130 to 160 loads) and digs out about 9.3 cubic yards, about $370, and infill runs 500 to 1,000 pounds for a lawn against 1,000 to 2,000 pounds for a recreational green or 2,500 to 3,500 pounds for a professional-style one.
quote: Note: You will need about 1 ton of aggregate or base material for every 100 sq. ft. at a 3” depth. … For each ton of aggregate, you are looking at approximately 13-16 wheelbarrows full
source_label: Worked example on SYNLawn's base and sand rates, SGW's 6-inch green base, Motz's infill rates and Larimer County's 2026 rubble fee
notes: Inputs: backyard-putting-green-cost.synlawn-diy-lawn-base (1 ton per 100 sq ft at 3 in; 13-16 loads a ton; 1-2 lb sand per sq ft), backyard-putting-green-cost.sgw-base-and-contours (6-inch minimum), backyard-putting-green-cost.motz-infill-rates (2-4 and 5-7 lb per sq ft), backyard-putting-green-cost.larimer-rubble-fee-2026 ($40 per cubic yard, L x W x H / 27). 500 is Southwest Greens' usual residential size (backyard-putting-green-size.swg-backyard-green-sizes). Lawn: 500/100 = 5 tons; 5 x 13 = 65, 5 x 16 = 80 loads; 500 x 0.25 ft = 125 cu ft / 27 = 4.63 cu yd; x $40 = $185.19. Green: 6 in = twice the 3-inch rate = 10 tons; 130 to 160 loads; 500 x 0.5 = 250 cu ft / 27 = 9.26 cu yd; x $40 = $370.37. Assumes the dig matches the base depth (SYNLawn: 'remove between 3”- 4” to create an adequate drainage base') and that the rock weighs the same per inch at 6 inches as at 3. Volumes are measured in the ground; excavated soil loosens, so a load can measure more. State surcharge not included. Infill: lawn 500 x 1-2 = 500-1,000 lb; recreational 500 x 2-4 = 1,000-2,000 lb; professional-style 500 x 5-7 = 2,500-3,500 lb, before Motz's separate top dressing.
